title: How to give negative feedback well
author: Luca Foppoli
summary: Foppoli adapts Marshall Rosenberg's Nonviolent Communication into a four-step sequence a manager can run in a difficult conversation: observation, feelings, need, request. His structural claim is that the order is not optional, because the first two steps earn the right to be heard and the last two spend the credit just earned. Step one insists on facts stated in the first person, so that the conversation is not two people arguing about a movie they watched separately, and it is finished only when both parties agree on what happened. Step two requires the manager to own the emotion rather than attribute it, and Foppoli is blunt that a situation does not make you angry, you chose anger. Steps three and four move from the underlying need to a specific request, including a written recap from the report that creates a record in his own words. He also sets a boundary on negotiation: a manager communicates the needs of the role rather than bargaining over standards. The piece closes with two side effects of preparing this way, namely that a jumbled grievance often collapses into clarity, and sometimes into the recognition that the case does not stand at all.
points: The four steps are presented as a load-bearing sequence with explicit done-when conditions for each, not as a menu of techniques.
Each step is illustrated by a scripted exchange with a senior report who cannot answer questions about his own customer, including the pushback a manager should expect.
Foppoli draws a hard line between owning your feelings and outsourcing them, telling readers to grow up and take responsibility for their own choices.
The written recap requested at step four functions as both a comprehension check and a documented trace of the conversation.
He frames preparation as diagnostic: working the four steps in advance can reveal that the feedback conversation should not happen at all.
quotes: Remember: you control the delivery, not the reception. Your job is to deliver the message respectfully and clearly, but he chooses whether to change his behavior.
In step 1 and 2 you earn the right to be heard; In step 3 and 4 you spend the currency you just earned.
Its purpose is to ground the conversation in the same facts, lest it becomes two people debating how the movie ended after having watched two different movies.
Use the pronoun “I”: these are the feelings you chose to experience and the other person, while responsible for his behavior, is not responsible for them.
The situation did not “make you angry”: the situation was the situation and you chose to respond with anger. Grow up and take responsibility for your own choices.
You are the manager and you are communicating the needs of the role, not negotiating your standards.
This surfaces any unclear point and creates a trace, in his own words, that the conversation has taken place.

What initially resembles a jumbled mess of judgments and feelings will start looking simple and linear. You might even decide to avoid the feedback conversation altogether because the case does not stand.
